items.title: A time you failed at something important
qs: Describe a time when you failed at something important.
What happened and why did you fail?
How did this failure affect your future?
items.note: Repeated again this week, now with 'how it affected your future'. Finish with a clear lesson you learned.
model: I'd like to talk about the time I failed my first attempt at a national English exam, which turned out to be one of the most useful setbacks of my life.

It happened two years ago. I had studied grammar for months, but I hardly practised speaking or timed writing. On the day, I ran out of time in the writing section and froze during the speaking interview, so my score was well below what I needed.
Looking back, the main reason I failed was poor preparation strategy rather than a lack of effort. I was studying hard but not studying smart, and I never tested myself under real exam conditions.

The failure changed my future in a positive way. I joined a study group, recorded myself speaking every day and wrote two timed essays a week. Six months later I passed with a much higher score and won a place at university.
Since then, I have treated mistakes as feedback rather than as a disaster. That experience taught me persistence, and I honestly believe I would not be where I am now without it.

items.title: A time you shared a secret
qs: Describe a time when you shared a secret with someone.
Who did you share it with and why?
How did you feel afterwards?
items.note: A favourite topic in recent sessions. Choose a harmless secret, such as a surprise or a plan, so the story is easy to tell.
model: I'm going to describe a time when I shared a secret with my older sister about a surprise party for our parents' anniversary.

My brother and I had been planning it for weeks, but we realised we couldn't organise the food and the guest list without help, so I told my sister everything one evening and made her promise not to say a word.
I chose her because she is very reliable and good at keeping things to herself. She immediately offered to take care of the cooking, which took a huge weight off my shoulders.

Afterwards I felt relieved and a little nervous at the same time, because the more people know a secret, the easier it is to slip out. Luckily she kept her promise, and our parents were completely surprised.
The experience showed me that sharing a secret with the right person can actually make a plan stronger, as long as you trust them completely.

items.title: A happy moment or event
qs: Describe a happy moment or event in your life.
When and where did it happen?
Why did it make you so happy?
items.note: Back again after a month. Use feeling words: thrilled, over the moon, proud, relieved.
model: One of the happiest moments of my life was the day I found out I had been accepted to university.
It was a hot afternoon last August. I was at home with my family when the results appeared online, and my hands were shaking as I typed in my number.
When I saw my name on the list, I screamed so loudly that our neighbours came to check on us. My mother burst into tears, and my father, who rarely shows emotion, gave me a big hug.
It made me so happy because it was the reward for two years of hard work, early mornings and many sacrifices. I also felt proud that I had made my parents proud.
Even now, whenever I feel tired or unmotivated, I remember that moment and it reminds me that effort really does pay off.

items.title: An important decision you made
qs: Describe an important decision you made.
Why was it difficult to make?
How do you feel about it now?
items.note: The Nukus report gave only part of the wording, so prepare a story that fits 'difficult', 'important' or 'regretted' decisions.
model: I'd like to talk about the decision to change my field of study from economics to English teaching.
It was difficult because my parents had always imagined me working in a bank, and economics seemed like the safer choice for a stable salary. I was worried about disappointing them.

I spent weeks weighing up the pros and cons. In the end I talked openly with my family, explained how much I enjoyed helping my classmates with English, and showed them that teachers are in high demand.
Now I feel it was absolutely the right choice. I enjoy my studies, my results are much better, and my parents are proud of me.
The experience taught me that an important decision should be based on your strengths and interests, not only on what others expect.

items.title: A time you felt stronger
qs: Describe a time when you felt stronger than before.
What made you feel stronger?
How did this experience change you?
items.note: New this week. 'Stronger' can mean mentally strong. A story about overcoming a difficulty works best.
model: I'd like to describe the time I felt much stronger after finishing my first half-marathon last spring.
For years I believed I was not a sporty person, and I could barely run for ten minutes. A friend persuaded me to join a running club, and we trained three times a week for four months.
What made me feel stronger was not only my fitness but crossing the finish line after twenty-one kilometres. My legs were aching, but I realised I could do far more than I had thought.
This experience changed my attitude to challenges in general. Now, when I face a difficult exam or a busy week, I tell myself that if I could finish that race, I can manage this too.
So it made me physically fitter, but more importantly it made me mentally tougher and more confident.

items.title: Should society move to a four-day working week?
qs: Society should move from a five-day to a four-day working week. Discuss the arguments for and against.
items.note: New this week. Give two points on each side, then a clear opinion.
for: Better work-life balance and mental health
Rested staff are often more productive
Less commuting means less traffic and pollution
against: Some services (hospitals, shops) must stay open
Longer daily hours can cause tiredness
model: Many countries are now experimenting with a four-day working week, and it is a controversial issue.
On the one hand, a shorter week gives people more time for their families, hobbies and rest, which can reduce stress and burnout.
Furthermore, several trials have shown that well-rested employees often get the same amount of work done in four days, so productivity does not necessarily fall.
On the other hand, not every job can be shortened. Hospitals, shops and public transport need staff every day, so this system is difficult to apply everywhere.
In addition, if the same hours are squeezed into four days, the working day becomes longer and people may feel exhausted, and small businesses could lose customers.
In my opinion, a four-day week is a good idea for office jobs where results matter more than hours, but it should be introduced gradually and flexibly rather than for everyone at once.

items.title: Private cars vs bicycles in cities
qs: People in cities should use bicycles instead of private cars. Discuss the arguments for and against.
items.note: New this week, and the same theme appeared in an IELTS Writing task on 21 Nov. Related to the logged 'private cars banned in city centres' essay.
for: Much cheaper than owning a car
against: Hard in very hot or cold weather
Not practical for long distances or families
model: Whether city residents should choose bicycles over cars is an important question as our cities become more crowded.
One strong argument for bicycles is the environment. Bikes produce no exhaust fumes, so if more people cycled, air quality and traffic jams would both improve.
Another advantage is health and cost. Cycling to work is free daily exercise, and it saves the large expense of fuel, insurance and parking.
However, cycling can be dangerous in cities without proper bike lanes, where cyclists have to share the road with fast cars and buses.
Moreover, bicycles are not practical for everyone. Elderly people, parents with small children or anyone travelling long distances in extreme heat or snow will still need a car.
Overall, I believe bicycles should be encouraged for short trips, but only if the government first builds safe bike lanes; cars will still be necessary for some journeys.

items.title: Nature documentaries raise environmental awareness
qs: Nature documentaries are an effective way to raise awareness of environmental problems. Discuss the arguments for and against.
items.note: Repeated after a month. Mention a real example of a documentary you have watched.
against: Viewers forget quickly and do not change habits
Some films focus on beauty, not problems
People who watch them already care
model: Nature documentaries have become extremely popular, and many people believe they help protect the planet.
First, these films show problems that most of us never see with our own eyes, such as melting ice or plastic in the ocean, and strong images can change people's attitudes.
Second, documentaries on television and streaming platforms reach millions of viewers, including children, who may later choose careers in science or conservation.
On the other hand, many viewers feel sad for an hour and then forget, without changing their daily habits like using less plastic.
Also, the people who choose to watch these films are often those who already care about nature, so the message may not reach the people who need it most.
In my view, documentaries are a useful starting point, but they work best when combined with education in schools and practical action by governments.

items.title: Smartphones should be banned in classrooms
qs: Smartphones should be banned in classrooms. Discuss the arguments for and against.
items.note: One of the most repeated Part 3 topics, reported this week in Namangan. Students at our centre should know this one well.
against: Needed to contact parents in emergencies
Students must learn to use technology responsibly
model: Whether smartphones should be banned from classrooms is a hot topic for schools around the world.
Supporters of a ban argue that phones are a huge distraction. Notifications and social media make it very hard for students to concentrate on the lesson.
They also point out that phones make cheating easier and reduce real conversation between classmates during breaks.
However, smartphones can be excellent learning tools. Students can use online dictionaries, educational apps and search for information quickly.
In addition, many parents want their children to be reachable in an emergency, and a total ban does not teach young people to manage technology responsibly.
Personally, I support a middle way: phones should be switched off and kept in bags during lessons, but teachers can allow them for specific learning tasks.

items.title: A university degree is no longer ... (reported incomplete)
qs: A university degree is no longer ... (the candidate did not remember the end; most likely 'necessary for success'). Discuss the arguments for and against.
items.note: Reported in two posts but the statement was cut off. Prepare the 'degree vs skills and experience' arguments; they also fit the 7 Nov Writing Task 2.
for: Many successful people have no degree
against: Doctors, lawyers and engineers must have degrees
University builds critical thinking and networks
model: Some people now claim that a university degree is no longer necessary for success, especially with so many online learning options.
Those who agree point to famous entrepreneurs and IT specialists who built careers without a degree, which shows that talent and hard work matter most.
They also argue that many employers now care more about practical skills and certificates, which can be gained quickly and cheaply online.
On the other hand, many professions, such as medicine, law and engineering, are impossible without a formal degree, for obvious safety reasons.
Furthermore, statistics in most countries show that graduates still earn more on average, and university develops critical thinking and useful contacts.
In my opinion, a degree is still very valuable, but it is no longer the only path; the best results come from combining a degree with practical experience.
